Abstract 36

In neuroimaging research, efforts to enhance replication and reproducibility have 37

increased the focus on improving transparency, particularly in the complex data analysis 38

processes. We conducted a multi-lab collaborative study involving 38 international teams 39

that analyzed two functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS) datasets. These teams 40

tested seven group-level and forty individual-level hypotheses, and they submitted 41

detailed reports on their analysis pipelines and testing outcomes. The results showed 42

significant variability in hypothesis testing outcomes due to differences in analytical 43

approaches. There was greater consensus in group-level analyses compared to 44

individual-level analyses. Factors such as the pruning method, hemodynamic response 45

function model and estimation, and statistical analysis space partly account for the 46

variability in hypothesis testing outcomes. Additionally, we have found higher similarity in 47

hypothesis testing outcomes across the researchers who reported higher confidence in 48

their analysis skills. This study underscores the importance of complying with best 49

practices in fNIRS analysis methodologies and the need for standardized analysis 50

protocols to improve reliability and credibility. 51

1 Introduction 52

Failures to replicate or reproduce published work have raised major concerns across 53

several fields in science (1–3). These reports have catalyzed both meta-research to explore 54

the factors leading to diminished replication and reproduction rates (4–8), and the launch 55

of initiatives focused on improving these critical aspects of scientific research (9–11). In 56

particular, the field of functional neuroimaging has progressively intensified its efforts to 57

address the challenges of replicability and reproducibility (12,13). 58

A significant part of the problem in neuroimaging relates to the complexity of the 59

analysis. As neuroimaging data analysis has grown increasingly complex over recent 60

(14,15) decades, it has become essential to ensure transparency in reporting analysis 61

details to support reproducibility (12,16–19). Current analysis pipelines encompass multiple 62

stages, including data selection criteria, preprocessing options, selection of data elements 63

(e.g., regions of interest), subsequent post-processing options, and an array of statistical 64

models for hypothesis testing, with a multitude of parameters for each of these stages (14). 65


<!-- Page 6 -->


This diversity in processing and analysis options provides considerable flexibility in 66

analyzing the same dataset in various ways (15,16,19), thereby enabling the exploration of a 67

broader spectrum of research questions and accommodating different assumptions. 68

While analytical flexibility represents a significant advancement in the evolution of 69

quantitative science, especially in handling high-dimensional data, it also poses 70

challenges. Varying analysis pipelines can produce markedly divergent results, potentially 71

leading to altered interpretations or even contradictory outcomes (15,20,21). Analytical 72

flexibility also leads to analytical variability: when researchers can select from a broad 73

spectrum of possible and justifiable analytical options, they are likely to make different 74

choices. This freedom diminishes the comparability of results between studies, even 75

within the same study (22–27). Moreover, due to the extensive array of preprocessing and 76

analysis options, researchers might be inclined to initially test pipelines aligning most with 77

their expectations and exclusively report these outcomes. This approach, influenced by 78

expectation and selection bias, results in undisclosed manipulation of analytical flexibility, 79

ultimately undermining its reliability and credibility (13). 80

Experiments conducted in collaboration with research communities have been 81

instrumental in assessing the impact of analytical variability. In these studies, researchers 82

are given the same data set and test pre-specified hypotheses using analytical methods 83

that they consider most suitable. Such experiments have been conducted with some 84

neuroimaging techniques, including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and 85

electroencephalography (EEG), and they have shown that researchers use a wide array of 86

analysis pipelines, which can lead to substantial differences in the reported findings and 87

conclusions drawn from the same data (25,26,28–32). 88

Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS) is another neuroimaging tool that has 89

seen significant growth over the past decades. This optical imaging method utilizes near- 90

infrared light to measure changes in brain hemoglobin concentrations (33–35). The 91

portability, ease of use, and relatively low cost of fNIRS, compared to fMRI, highlight its 92

substantial potential for routine use in scientific, clinical, and commercial settings, 93

especially in populations or experimental paradigms where fMRI is less suitable. This 94

adaptability allows for more complex paradigms with high ecological validity and low 95

restrictions on natural movements and behaviors, introducing additional variability into 96


<!-- Page 7 -->


data analysis.  Moreover, the ongoing development of new hardware and analytical 97

pipelines contributes to this variability. 98

Despite sharing similarities with EEG and fMRI, fNIRS has unique features and has been 99

used in experimental designs that necessitate careful consideration regarding analytical 100

flexibility. Directly applying conclusions from other techniques to fNIRS is not 101

straightforward. As the adoption of fNIRS expands across various fields, research at the 102

community level is needed to assess a) how analytical variability manifests concerning the 103

spectrum of analytical choices and b) how these different choices affect analysis results 104

and conclusions that can be drawn from identical fNIRS data. Initial investigations suggest 105

considerable analytical variability across fNIRS pipeline settings (36–38). However, a 106

detailed analysis focusing on this variability within fNIRS has yet to be conducted. 107

Building upon previous investigations, the present study explored the wide-ranging 108

analysis methods employed within the fNIRS research community. By extending previous 109

efforts, we quantified the variability in results when different researchers assessed the 110

same dataset both at the group and individual levels. Given the complexity of 111

experimental protocols and data analysis pipelines and the lack of standardization in fNIRS 112

research (39,40), understanding these variations is essential for progress. More 113

importantly, addressing such variability in a period of increasing fNIRS significance in 114

neuroscience is a crucial step toward establishing standards in the field. 115

For this purpose, this study invited members from the global fNIRS community to 116

participate in a multi-lab analysis experiment. Researchers were provided with two fNIRS 117

datasets, a brief description of the experimental protocols, and a list of pre-defined 118

group-level and individual-level hypotheses related to research questions that could be 119

investigated with these datasets. Researchers were tasked to test these hypotheses. 120

Importantly, researchers were not provided with instructions on how to perform these 121

tasks other than based on their own expertise and best judgment. The first dataset 122

(Dataset I) comprised fNIRS recordings obtained from an auditory paradigm, which 123

included speech, auditory noise stimuli, and silence, each lasting approximately 5 124

seconds. The hypotheses for this dataset involved group-level analysis. The second 125

dataset (Dataset II) came from a motor experiment where participants performed 126

repeated right- and left-hand finger tapping for 2 and 3 seconds. The hypotheses for this 127


<!-- Page 8 -->


dataset were focused on individual-level analysis. In both cases, the inter-stimulus 128

interval varied randomly between 10 and 20 seconds. 129

After completing data analysis, researchers were asked to submit their results using a 130

specifically designed form that inquired about the statistical outcomes for all pre-specified 131

hypotheses. In a follow-up questionnaire, researchers were requested to provide further 132

details about their analysis pipeline, including specifics about preprocessing and analysis 133

steps they had performed. In this work, we synthesize and interpret the diversity of 134

analysis approaches within the fNIRS community and discuss their potential implications 135

for research outcomes based on data obtained through this collaborative effort. 136

Of the 223 researchers who initially registered for the study, 102 ultimately submitted 139

Statistical Analysis Choices 172

outcomes for hypothesis testing, we examined the choices made at various stages of fNIRS 174

2.3 Choice of Analysis Pipeline Affects Hypothesis Testing Outcomes 261

We investigated the effect of the choice of the major analysis steps on resultant 262

hypothesis testing outcomes across teams using a logistic regression approach. The results 263

reveal differential impacts of these processing steps on the logistic regression fit, with 264

significance determined at a threshold of p < 0.05. Table 1 summarizes the number of 265

hypotheses for which each distinct category under each analysis step significantly explains 266

the variation in hypothesis testing outcomes across teams. Notably, for the HRF Estimation 267

step, "Block Averaging" emerged with nine significant contributions, considering “GLM” as 268

the reference category. Similarly, for the HRF Regressor, “Flexible” and “None” (i.e., block 269

averaging, which does not have any HRF Regressor), each emerged with four significant 270

contributions, with “Fixed” as the reference category. (Please note that, for the regression 271

analysis, we merged the HRF regressor categories “Consecutive Gaussians” and “FIR 272

3 Discussion 388

Noninvasive neuroimaging techniques have revolutionized our understanding of the 389

human brain, opening up new avenues in various scientific fields. As technology has 390

advanced, facilitating more flexible experimental protocols, it has also increased analytical 391

variability in data analysis, affecting the consistency of conclusions drawn from 392

neuroimaging techniques, as seen with fMRI and EEG. 393


<!-- Page 20 -->


Our results show that fNIRS faces similar challenges. Over the past decade, fNIRS has 394

become a reliable and widely adopted tool (35), particularly in experiments where other 395

techniques fall short, due to its flexibility and lower operational threshold compared to 396

fMRI. However, while it is easy to acquire interpretable signals, assessing their 397

meaningfulness remains difficult. In addition, rapid technological advances have outpaced 398

the standardization of data analysis, making it crucial to understand how different analysis 399

pipelines impact scientific consistency. The results presented in this work shine light on 400

this issue and provides insights for other neuroimaging techniques by exploring the 401

influence of analytical flexibility and other key factors that contribute to variability in 402

outcomes, such as researcher confidence. 403

Overall, we observed high variability across teams in hypothesis testing, particularly at 404

the individual level. It is important to note that, because the data came from different 405

sources, any direct comparison between group- and individual-level agreement is prone 406

to bias from confounding factors such as variations in data quality. Despite this limitation, 407

higher agreement (> 80%) was predominantly seen in most group-level hypotheses (5 out 408

of 7 hypotheses). In contrast, only two hypotheses achieved similar agreement at the 409

individual level, and in only two out of 10 participants. This discrepancy is a consequence 410

of the nature of group- versus individual-level analysis: while group-level analysis focuses 411

on common effects and treats individual variations as noise or measurement error, 412

individual-level analysis is more sensitive to intrinsic differences in anatomy and 413

physiology. This sensitivity makes individual outcomes more dependent on specific 414

choices in the analysis pipeline (e.g., exclusion criteria resulting in the removal of different 415

trials and/or fNIRS channels across subjects). 416

No two teams adopted identical workflows, echoing findings from a previous study on 417

variability in fMRI (25). The flexibility in choosing analysis pipelines led to considerable 418

differences in the methods used, particularly in signal preprocessing and statistical testing. 419

Recent efforts to establish best practices aim to enhance reproducibility, particularly for 420

these stages (39). For instance, the impact of confounding systemic signals on fNIRS is 421

well-recognized, along with the importance of methodologically addressing these by 422

including additional systemic information in the analysis whenever possible, such as 423

short-channel measurements as proxies for systemic physiology, which can greatly 424

reduce false discovery rates (42,43). Many groups (79%) used GLM for regression of 425


<!-- Page 21 -->


systemic signals, while only a few (20%) used less robust methods like block averaging, 426

which does not account for systemic physiological effects. 427

Among GLM users, a slight majority (46% versus 33%) opted for AR-IRLS over OLS, as 428

it effectively reduces false positives by accounting for the intrinsic temporal correlation of 429

fNIRS signals through autoregressive models with optimal order selection (44). Choices for 430

the HRF regressor varied across six variants, from those allowing extensive shape fitting 431

like the FIR model, to those with minimal parameters such as the Canonical model. This 432

variety highlights the need to establish a consensus on selecting HRF regressors. Regarding 433

the additional regressors to the HRF, 70% of the groups that employed GLM used short- 434

channel-based information. 435

It is also worth noting that the majority of groups applied temporal smoothing (90%) to 436

the fNIRS signal, using band-pass (70%) or low-pass (20%) filtering. Therefore, these filter 437

weights need to be accommodated in the estimation of temporal correlation with GLM 438

(39,44). Ignoring these correlations can lead to biased estimates of degrees of freedom 439

and standard error, thereby invalidating statistical tests. 440

A slight majority (52%) used HbO for statistical testing, as it generally shows a stronger 441

response than HbR, though it is more susceptible to task-related systemic physiological 442

changes (38), potentially leading to a higher false discovery rate. Groups also varied in 443

their approach to defining the signal space for statistical testing, with 53% using Regions of 444

Interest (ROIs) to reduce spontaneous noise and improve reliability, while 29% conducted 445

their analyses at the channel level, which can increase sensitivity to spatial variability, 446

especially in studies with low-density fNIRS setups lacking detailed spatial information. 447

Pre-experiment optode registration can reduce this issue by ensuring consistent 448

placement of optodes, thus enhancing reproducibility (45). When anatomical registration 449

is properly performed, translating data from the channel space to either the ROI or voxel 450

spaces generally results in less variability (46,47). A small amount (15%) utilized a 451

combination of both ROI and channel-based methods. 452

Additionally, 52% of all groups did not perform multiple comparisons correction, 453

increasing the risk of false positives (42,43). The statistical tests of this study were based 454

on measurements from multichannel fNIRS systems (e.g., 64 source-detector 455

combinations, or channels, were used for the motor dataset. When a significance 456

threshold of uncorrected p = 0.05 was applied, on average, 5% of the 64 channels (i.e., 3 457


<!-- Page 22 -->


channels) could be false positives). The number of false positives increases even further 458

when using voxels in the case of reconstructed image space from diffuse optical 459

tomography or interpolating kernels. This issue, referred to as the multiple testing 460

problem, can be addressed using methods that control the family-wise error rate at level 461

(e.g., corrected p = 0.05), such as Benjamini-Hochberg, Bonferroni correction, or random 462

field theory (48). These methods calculate the probability that t-values exceed a given 463

threshold across a set of channels, voxels, or clusters. 464

Our logistic regression analysis revealed that variability in hypothesis testing outcomes 465

was partially explained by the choices at different stages of data processing, particularly 466

methods for data pruning and the choices for HRF estimation, HRF regressor, signal space 467

for statistical testing, and the use of multiple comparisons correction. Specifically, opting 468

for block averaging rather than a GLM in HRF estimation contributed to the variability in 469

the hypothesis outcomes. Similarly, the choice of performing statistical testing on 470

individual channels over ROIs explained some of the variability in the hypothesis 471

outcomes. 472

When we break down the hypothesis testing results by self-reported confidence, 473

higher confidence was associated with more consistent results at the group level. While 474

confidence is often linked to higher decision-making accuracy (49), we cannot 475

conclusively attribute these observed consistencies to result accuracy without further 476

validation, such as using a synthetic dataset with known ground truth. Confidence was 477

also significantly correlated with the average number of years of fNIRS experience of the 478

team members, suggesting that lower variability in hypothesis testing outcomes may be 479

due to fewer errors in analysis pipelines and/or convergence towards certain analysis 480

methods as experience in the field increases. 481

The broader utilization of GLM as an HRF estimation method among the groups that 482

showed high similarity in hypothesis testing outcomes and who at the same time reported 483

high confidence indicates a preference for robust statistical frameworks that may better 484

accommodate the confounding signals in the fNIRS data. The inclusion of short-separation 485

(SS) regression techniques by a significant majority of this group further supports this. The 486

pronounced difference in the use of Gamma HRF Regressors between this group and the 487

rest of the groups (30.8% vs 4.3%) points towards a methodological divergence in 488

addressing hemodynamic response modeling. 489


<!-- Page 23 -->


It is worth noting that a few aspects of our study design should be considered before 490

generalizing the findings above. First, the recruitment of researchers was based on an 491

open call, and while the sample was diverse and global, certain regions, particularly Asia, 492

were underrepresented. The datasets were chosen based on their availability and 493

adherence to current best practices in fNIRS acquisition. We selected the finger-tapping 494

task for its standard use in fNIRS, ensuring familiarity among researchers and offering little 495

novelty from a neuroscience perspective. Similarly, auditory stimulation is a primary brain 496

function and is expected to yield more consistency than cognitive tasks, for example, even 497

though it is less common in fNIRS. These choices were intended to minimize other sources 498

of variability unrelated to analysis pipelines. However, both datasets used a similar block 499

design with short stimulation times and had been previously published, which may have 500

introduced anchor bias, despite instructions not to consult the original results. The short 501

task durations also resulted in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), potentially affecting 502

pipelines differently and contributing to dataset-specific variability. Lastly, the formulation 503

of the hypotheses might have influenced analytical choices. Although we aimed to provide 504

clear, objective hypotheses for testing and offered an open forum for clarifications, varying 505

interpretations across groups could lead to differences in testing and reporting. 506

Taken together, our findings suggest substantial levels of analytical variability in fNIRS, 507

moderated by researchers’ experience and confidence. Researchers use the degrees of 508

freedom available in analyzing complex, high-dimensional fNIRS datasets, some of which 509

were identified only after specifically querying them in a follow-up questionnaire.  These 510

results strongly support earlier calls to increase transparency and adoption of open- 511

science practices to enhance the reproducibility and replicability in fNIRS research 512

(19,39,40). Implementing standardized protocols and parameter choices will help reduce 513

variability and enhance reproducibility, particularly in typical functional neuroimaging 514

protocols. However, it is important to recognize that consistency and reproducibility in 515

outcomes do not equate to accuracy, as consistent results do not automatically reflect 516

"ground truth". Moving forward, future efforts should shift from describing variability to 517

assessing the accuracy of data analysis pipelines and evaluating how different processing 518

steps influence how closely the results align with expected outcomes. 519

The fNIRS community has achieved significant milestones, with efforts to establish 520

best practice recommendations (19,39), common data structure standards (50,51), and 521


<!-- Page 24 -->


guidelines for study preregistration (40). Study preregistration and Registered Reports 522

(RRs) promote transparent study planning and reporting (40,52) by allowing the distinction 523

of planned hypothesis tests from exploratory analyses and mitigating false positive and 524

negative findings (53,54). Recent meta-research further provided evidence that they will 525

likely reduce publication bias (1,55) and enhance replicability of published research (56). 526

However, only about 1 in 500 fNIRS studies (0.2 %) is preregistered (57). 527

Data and code sharing should be encouraged as they allow researchers to reproduce 528

and replicate published work or test new hypotheses. While tools to do so are 529

increasingly available (19), more community efforts are required for their successful, 530

widespread use, along with appropriate training opportunities at various levels to help 531

researchers effectively and responsibly utilize these tools. 532

Moreover, global data pooling initiatives such as consortia would greatly increase 533

possibilities for meta-analytical and mega-analytical research. Global consortia such as 534

ENIGMA (Enhancing NeuroImaging Genetics through Meta Analysis) have become the gold 535

standard in other fields such as clinical MRI research (58,59). Consortia can aggregate 536

large sample sizes and test and standardize data-quality control procedures. They yield 537

robust, generalizable results, which has also motivated other imaging fields such as EEG to 538

form consortia (60). Similar developments would be desirable for fNIRS research (39,40). 539

Lastly, adopting these tools requires a cultural shift in the fNIRS community that must 540

be supported by key stakeholders, including academic societies and institutions, through 541

educational initiatives within the community (1,61). Without such collective effort, the full 542

potential of these advancements cannot be achieved. 543

4.4.3 Logistic Regression 672

The relationship between the analysis steps (independent variables) and the 673

hypothesis testing outcomes (dependent variable) across teams was investigated using a 674

binary logistic regression. The outcome of hypothesis testing was indicated by a binary 675

variable, as reported by each team. As each independent variable includes multiple sub- 676

categories (e.g., filtering can be divided into four categories - band-pass, high-pass, low- 677

pass, and no filtering), we selected the most-commonly chosen category by the teams as 678

the reference category. The logistic regression model was performed with the 'fitglm' 679

function in MATLAB. Given the binary nature of the dependent variable, the binomial 680

distribution was selected to appropriately model the response. The logistic link function, 681

specifically the logit link, was applied to establish the connection between the linear 682

predictor and the probability of observing a significant hypothesis testing outcome. This 683

analysis was performed separately for each of the 47 hypotheses (7 at the group level and 684

40 at the individual level [i.e., 4 individual-level hypotheses X 10 subjects]). 685

We also employed multiple logistic regression to account for multiple independent 686

variables, each representing a distinct step in the analysis. This method allowed us to 687

assess the simultaneous impact of these analysis steps on the probability of obtaining a 688

significant result in hypothesis testing. Prior to multiple logistic regression, we tested any 689

multicollinearity between the processing pipeline steps that explain the variability in the 690

hypothesis testing outcomes significantly (i.e., Pruning, HRF Estimation Method, and Signal 691

Space) via a chi-squared test. This test is often applied to explore the association between 692

categorical independent variables by identifying significant relationships between pairs of 693

such variables. In this study, we conducted contingency table analysis to generate 694

frequency distribution tables that illustrate the joint occurrences of categories for each pair 695

of categorical independent variables. Subsequently, the chi-square test of independence 696


<!-- Page 31 -->


was applied to evaluate the presence of significant associations between the categorical 697

variables, which yielded both a test statistic and a p-value. 698

We established a p-value threshold of 0.05 for both the logistic regression analysis 699

and the chi-square test. We did not perform any multiple comparison corrections. 700

4.4.4 Visualization of Processing Steps 701

We used Sankey diagrams (Python) to visualize essential processing steps and 702

parameters the participating groups employed for signal analysis and statistical testing 703

(Figs. 4 and 5, Section 2.3). The reported choice of methods, parameters, or regressors are 704

encoded as nodes in the diagram. Each node belongs to one of several categories (for 705

instance, a category of methods, such as “Artifact Rejection”), which make up the 706

diagram’s vertical stages. This visualization enables both a quantitative and a qualitative 707

assessment of the (co)occurrence and divergence of methodological choices across 708

stages/categories in the analyses. It should be pointed out that the implied directionality of 709

the stages is primarily a logical and not a temporal one and thus not strictly directional (for 710

instance: “Motion Artifact Rejection” typically follows “Pruning”; the choice of a method for 711

HRF estimation precedes the choice of a solver and the choice of regressors). The data 712

was conditioned as follows before the construction of the Sankey diagrams:  1) Missing 713

inputs, i.e., fields that were left empty and not reported otherwise by the researchers, 714

were interpreted and categorized as a step not performed (e.g., no response in “Method 715

used for artifact removal” implied no motion artifact removal performed). 2) Functionally 716

equal or highly similar categories or nodes were joined (e.g., in “Quality Assessment and 717

Pruning”, “Manual Selection” and “Visual Inspection of Time Domain” were joined into 718

“Manual Pruning”). 3) In some categories, multiple choices and combinations of methods 719

were reported. To account for this, we report the absolute frequencies of each method in 720

% (i.e., the number of users that made that choice as a fraction of all users) and separately 721

report numbers for both its individual use and its use in combination with others. 722

Groups reported using “default settings” for methods and parameters from different 723

frequency and intersections of categories for which the use of default settings was 725
